body:
From a large empire to competing centres of power

The Mughal Empire reached great territorial extent under Aurangzeb (1658–1707), but controlling distant provinces became increasingly difficult. Mughal decline means the weakening of the emperor's ability to command officials, collect revenue and enforce decisions across the empire. It did not mean that every province became independent immediately in 1707.

Aurangzeb's prolonged campaigns in the Deccan consumed soldiers, money and administrative attention. Resistance from the Marathas continued despite Mughal victories against the Deccan sultanates. Elsewhere, Rajput conflicts and rebellions involving Jats, Sikhs and other groups put additional pressure on imperial authority. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, succession disputes and court rivalries made effective central control still harder.

Why the administrative system came under strain

The empire depended on mansabdars, officials ranked by a mansab. Their zat rank determined personal status and salary, while the sawar rank concerned the cavalrymen they were expected to maintain. Many were paid through jagirs, assignments of the right to receive revenue from specified lands. A jagir was not automatically personal ownership of that land.

As the number of mansabdars increased, suitable revenue assignments became scarce. Actual collections from some jagirs fell below the sums notionally assigned. Some jagirdars tried to collect more from cultivators during their tenure, increasing rural distress. The resulting jagirdari crisis weakened the balance between imperial service, military obligations and revenue.

In the provinces, the subadar was the governor, the diwan managed revenue, and faujdari referred to military and policing responsibilities. When powerful governors gained influence over these functions together, they could command troops, control collections and send less revenue to Delhi. Local zamindars and chiefs also took advantage of diminished imperial supervision.

Court factions and invasions

Competition among noble factions, notably the Iranis and Turanis, weakened later emperors. Foreign invasions then exposed the empire's vulnerability. Nadir Shah of Iran sacked Delhi in 1739. The Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Abdali, also called Ahmad Shah Durrani, made repeated incursions into north India between 1748 and 1761. These attacks were serious blows, but internal administrative and military weaknesses had developed earlier.

Prelims focus

  • 1707: death of Aurangzeb, a key chronological marker for rapid eighteenth-century political change.
  • Mansab: rank; jagir: revenue assignment, not necessarily land ownership.
  • Zat: personal rank and salary; sawar: cavalry responsibility.
  • 1739: Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi.
  • 1748–1761: repeated invasions by Ahmad Shah Abdali.
  • Trap: the Mughal Empire did not vanish as a political institution in 1707; authority passed gradually to regional powers.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, “The Mughal Empire”, printed pp. 51–55; Chapter 10, “Eighteenth-Century Political Formations”, printed pp. 138–142, 2020–21 edition.]

title: Why Mughal Imperial Authority Weakened after Aurangzeb

body:
Regional independence did not always mean a complete break with the emperor

As Mughal authority weakened, provincial governors, older ruling families and groups that had resisted imperial power established regional states. Some still used Mughal titles or acknowledged the emperor formally, while making most practical decisions themselves. Formal allegiance and effective political control must therefore be distinguished.

Three broad and overlapping types of states

  • Former Mughal provinces: Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad were consolidated by leading Mughal officials who became effectively autonomous.
  • Older autonomous principalities: Rajput rulers, notably those of Amber and Jodhpur, built on their watan jagirs, or hereditary territorial assignments, and sought neighbouring territory.
  • States strengthened by resistance: Marathas, Sikhs and Jats enlarged their authority through prolonged conflict with Mughal power.

The 3 prominent former Mughal provinces

RegionPrincipal rulerConsolidation of power
HyderabadNizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah; founded autonomous rule in 1724Controlled Deccan administration and appointments, while retaining a formal Mughal connection.
AwadhBurhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan; became subadar in 1722Brought political, financial and military functions under his authority and reorganised revenue collection.
BengalMurshid Quli KhanRose from revenue administration and deputy governorship; exercised a governor's powers without formally holding the subadari.

The three regimes drew strength from local resources. They often reduced reliance on older imperial jagirdars, used ijaradars (revenue farmers who contracted to pay a fixed sum for collection rights) and developed close relations with bankers and merchants. These measures made regional rulers more financially independent of Delhi, but they also changed who exercised control over cultivators and collections.

Other states to recognise

Rajput leaders including Ajit Singh of Jodhpur and Sawai Jai Singh of Amber sought wider political authority; Ajit Singh held the governorship of Gujarat, while Jai Singh held that of Malwa. Among Sikhs, armed bands developed into misls; dal khalsa referred to their combined forces. The Jat state of Bharatpur grew particularly strong under Suraj Mal. The Maratha state, arising from earlier resistance to Mughal rule, expanded further under the Peshwas.

Distinction: Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad are former Mughal provinces; the Rajput principalities represent older hereditary autonomy; the Marathas, Sikhs and Jats exemplify political formations strengthened through resistance. These categories describe origins, not rigid or permanent constitutional types.

Prelims focus

  • Hyderabad — Asaf Jah — 1724.
  • Awadh — Saadat Khan — 1722.
  • Bengal — Murshid Quli Khan — revenue administration.
  • Ijaradari: contracting out revenue collection to a revenue farmer.
  • Bharatpur — Jats — Suraj Mal; misls — Sikhs.
  • Trap: effective autonomy did not always end nominal allegiance to the Mughal emperor.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 10, “Eighteenth-Century Political Formations”, printed pp. 142–151, 2020–21 edition.]

pictures.alt: Regional states grouped by provincial autonomy, inherited watan jagirs and armed resistance, with formal Mughal allegiance compatible with practical autonomy.
pictures.caption: Different origins of regional political authority.

title: Regional States after Mughal Decline: Three Paths to Power

body:
What was swarajya?

Shivaji Bhosle established a Maratha kingdom in the seventeenth-century western Deccan. He was born at Shivneri Fort to Shahji Bhosle and Jijabai. His movement drew on local warrior families such as deshmukhs and the mobile fighting strength of the Maval region. The term swarajya means self-rule: here it describes a political territory governed under Shivaji's own authority rather than by the neighbouring sultanates or the Mughals. It should not be confused with the institutions of a modern democratic nation-state.

The Sahyadri or Western Ghats offered defensible passes and hill forts. The Konkan coast provided access to maritime routes, while the inland Desh linked the kingdom to the Deccan plateau. Shivaji combined forts, fast-moving forces, local support and diplomacy to confront stronger opponents, especially Bijapur and the Mughal Empire.

Main events in chronological order

YearEventWhy it matters
1659Conflict with Bijapur's general Afzal Khan at PratapgadHelped secure Shivaji's position in the western Deccan.
1664Raid on Surat, a wealthy Mughal port in GujaratDemonstrated the reach of a mobile Maratha force; it was a raid, not the lasting annexation of Surat.
1665Treaty of Purandar negotiated with Mughal commander Mirza Raja Jai SinghUnder Mughal military pressure Shivaji agreed to surrender 23 forts and retain 12 forts.
1666Visit to the Mughal court at Agra and subsequent escapeNegotiations with Aurangzeb broke down; Shivaji resumed independent action.
1674Coronation at Raigad as ChhatrapatiFormally asserted sovereign kingship.
1680Death of ShivajiResistance and state-building continued under his successors.

How to connect the events

Shivaji did not rely exclusively on pitched battles. His forces used mobility and knowledge of passes to surprise or evade larger armies. He also negotiated when circumstances demanded it, as at Purandar. The Agra episode in 1666 showed that an attempted accommodation with the Mughal court did not produce a lasting settlement. Coronation in 1674 asserted a separate royal authority, while institutions for revenue, army and forts supported the kingdom beyond individual campaigns.

Prelims focus

  • Shivneri: birthplace of Shivaji; Shahji and Jijabai: his parents.
  • 1659 — Pratapgad — Afzal Khan.
  • 1664 — Surat raid: Gujarat connection; not permanent occupation.
  • 1665 — Treaty of Purandar — Jai Singh: 23 forts surrendered, 12 retained.
  • 1666 — Agra episode; 1674 — Raigad coronation; 1680 — death.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 4, printed pp. 49–50, and Chapter 10, printed pp. 149–150; IGNOU, Rise of Marathas: Shivaji Maharaj, Unit 15, §§ 15.2–15.6 (consulted 19 November 2026); Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III: Maratha Period, Chapter 1, “Rise of the Maratha Power”, section on the Treaty of Purandar (consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Hill forts anchored Maratha power in the western Deccan.

title: Shivaji: Swarajya, Early Campaigns and Coronation

body:
King, ministers and accountability

Shivaji organised a monarchy in which the Chhatrapati held final authority. The principal ministerial arrangement is known as the Ashta Pradhan, or council of 8 high officers. Several of these offices had precedents in the Deccan sultanates; Shivaji reorganised them within his kingdom. They were not a modern cabinet whose collective decisions bound the ruler.

The ministers supervised departments and advised the king. Under Shivaji, their appointments generally depended on the ruler rather than automatic hereditary succession. They were ordinarily paid from the treasury rather than receiving personal revenue assignments in place of salaries. This helped the monarch retain control over public administration and military service.

The 8 offices and their duties

OfficeAlternative namePrincipal function
PeshwaMukhya PradhanChief minister; coordinated civil and military affairs.
AmatyaMazumdarState accounts, income and expenditure.
SachivSurnisOfficial documents and royal correspondence.
MantriWaqia-navisCourt records and the king's household affairs.
SumantDabirForeign relations and diplomacy.
SenapatiSarnobatCommand of the armed forces.
NyayadhishChief judgeJudicial affairs.
Pandit RaoDanadhyakshaReligious and charitable matters.

Do not confuse the Sachiv, responsible for state correspondence, with the Mantri, who maintained records connected with the court and royal household. Similarly, the Amatya handled accounts, whereas the Peshwa was the chief coordinating minister. The Senapati was a military office; the chief justice and Pandit Rao handled justice and religious affairs respectively.

Administrative units and local officers

Administration linked the court to prants (provinces), tarfs (local territorial units) and mauzas (villages). A subedar supervised a province, while local officials carried out collection and administration. Shivaji did not invent every title or territorial unit; he adapted existing Deccan practices while seeking closer supervision and more reliable collections.

Prelims focus

  • Ashta Pradhan: council of 8 ministers under Shivaji.
  • Peshwa: chief minister; Amatya: accounts; Sumant: diplomacy.
  • Sachiv: correspondence; Mantri: court records.
  • Senapati: army; Nyayadhish: justice; Pandit Rao: religious and charitable matters.
  • Trap: Shivaji's Ashta Pradhan advised the king, but its advice was not binding on him.

[IGNOU, Rise of the Marathas in the 17th Century, Unit 10, §§ 10.8.1–10.8.2; IGNOU, Rise of Marathas: Shivaji Maharaj, Unit 15, § 15.8; Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III: Maratha Period, Chapter 1, discussion of the Ashta Pradhan (all consulted 19 November 2026).]
